cim: Feeding The Machines: Who Pays For The Age Of Artificial Intelligence? – OpEd
cim_eredeti: Feeding The Machines: Who Pays For The Age Of Artificial Intelligence? – OpEd
szoveg_eredeti:
As AI demands more electricity, water and physical infrastructure, technological progress should be judged alongside the basic human needs that remain unmet.

Imagine two scenes after sunset. In one, a family is waiting for its first electricity connection, hoping that a child will soon be able to read under a dependable light. In the other, thousands of processors are being installed in a building designed to keep artificial intelligence available around the clock. The two places may be continents apart. Both belong to the same civilization, and both tell us something about what it is trying to build.

The machines we are creating do not need food or sleep. They do, however, require electricity to perform calculations, water or other means of cooling, minerals for their hardware and an industrial system capable of replacing that hardware. As AI becomes embedded in medicine, commerce and public services, those requirements will persist long after the excitement surrounding a new model has faded.

On November 19, the International Energy Agency (IEA) released its World Energy Outlook 2026, projecting that electricity consumption by data centers could roughly double to 1,000 terawatt-hours in 2030 under its Stated Policies Scenario. In October, the agency estimated that the largest data center operators would spend more than $700 billion in capital expenditure in 2026, predominantly on new facilities. The scale of the investment invites a question about the world in which those facilities will operate.

According to the United Nations’ 2026 assessment of Sustainable Development Goal 7, 655 million people, or 8% of the world’s population, lacked access to electricity in 2024. The IEA’s newer November outlook separately puts the number at around 720 million. These estimates should not be treated as a directly comparable year-to-year series. Using the UN’s 2024 figures gives us a common reference year for comparing basic services. Sub-Saharan Africa accounted for 86% of that year’s global electricity access gap.

On the same day that the IEA published its November outlook, the World Health Organization updated its global drinking-water assessment. In 2024, 2.1 billion people, approximately 26% of humanity, lacked safely managed drinking water. That does not mean they had no water at all: it means they did not have an improved source at home that was available when needed and protected from contamination. Among them, 106 million relied directly on untreated surface water. These populations may overlap with those lacking electricity; adding the two totals would misrepresent the scale of deprivation.

Neither statistic establishes that AI caused poverty or deprived a particular household of water. Many communities remain underserved because of inadequate infrastructure, conflict, weak institutions, limited investment and unaffordable services. Electricity available in a European industrial park cannot simply be delivered to a remote African village. Yet the contrast raises a legitimate question about which needs attract capital, engineering expertise and public attention, and how the benefits of technological progress are distributed.

The IEA’s latest outlook estimates that global data center activity consumed 885 billion liters of water in 2025, including 240 billion liters used directly in facilities. The larger figure also includes water consumed in electricity generation, chip manufacturing and primary energy supply. It covers data centers generally, rather than AI alone, and refers to water consumption rather than all water withdrawals. The same report places around 30% of existing and planned data center capacity in areas with high water stress.

AI is one important contributor to rising demand. The IEA’s 2026 energy and AI analysis projects that electricity use by AI-focused data centers could triple between 2025 and 2030. But local conditions determine the consequences. A facility drawing on spare grid capacity and responsibly sourced water poses a different problem from one in a drought-prone basin or on an overloaded network. New generation can expand supply; efficient chips and smaller models can reduce the resources needed for many tasks. Water-saving cooling designs may also require more electricity. The engineering choices matter.

There are powerful reasons to continue this research. The AlphaFold database makes more than 200 million protein structure predictions freely available, helping scientists investigate questions in biology and medicine. Research published in Nature in 2024 showed that AI could improve extreme river-flood forecasting in watersheds without local gauge measurements. Such work is particularly relevant to regions with limited observational infrastructure. These are examples of genuine scientific value, even if predictions still require appropriate validation and warnings must actually reach people at risk.

We should not treat every use of AI as equally valuable or equally resource intensive. The computation needed to investigate a disease, improve flood warnings or optimize a power network may have a very different public value from repeated generation of disposable content. There is no simple universal ranking, but developers and buyers can ask whether the resources consumed are proportionate to the benefit delivered. Efficiency gains are an opportunity to extend those benefits, not merely an invitation to increase consumption.

There is evidence that progress on basic infrastructure is possible. In June, the World Bank and African Development Bank reported that Mission 300 had helped connect more than 50 million people to electricity in 40 African countries. Its ambition is to reach 300 million by 2030. That effort requires very different investments from building a hyperscale computing facility, including local grids, decentralized generation and affordable household connections. The world needs the capacity to finance both.

Countries hosting data centers also have choices. Ireland’s electricity connection policy, announced in December 2025, requires new facilities seeking grid connections to provide corresponding generation or storage capacity and to source at least 80% of annual electricity demand from additional domestic renewable projects, with a transition period. It is one attempt to align digital investment with energy availability rather than assume that existing consumers can absorb every new demand.

Before approving major AI infrastructure, I would ask decision-makers to disclose its expected electricity and water demands, including seasonal peaks; establish who will pay for new utility capacity; and explain how essential household and public services will be protected during shortages. Commitments should be tested against drought, delayed grid expansion and weaker-than-expected commercial demand. Where public incentives are offered, communities should be able to see whether the promised benefits actually materialize.

No single investment can resolve the world’s inequities, and stopping AI development would not automatically deliver electricity or safe water to the people without them. But the success of this technological era deserves a wider measure than the size of a model or the valuation of the company that built it. We can pursue extraordinary advances in science while insisting that the resources sustaining those advances are managed responsibly.

We have learned to feed machines with electricity and teach them with the accumulated knowledge of generations. As their capabilities grow, the most meaningful evidence of our progress may still be found somewhere very ordinary: a household with a light that stays on, and a tap from which a child can safely drink.
